title: Years after Charleston church shooting, strength rises in a new memorial
text:
Years after Charleston church shooting, strength rises in a new memorial
A memorial at the Emanuel African Methodist Episcopal Church commemorates lives lost. It also shows a community meeting tragedy with love and hope.
Atlantic winds brought a chill into downtown Charleston, and rippled across a reflecting pool memorial for nine church members murdered during a Bible study over a decade ago.
Those winds also swept through pieces of paper held by Polly Sheppard. She was one of five survivors of the June 17, 2015, shooting at the Emanuel African Methodist Episcopal Church, which is the oldest congregation of its denomination in the South. The papers wavered, but Ms. Sheppard did not as she spoke during a ribbon cutting for the Emanuel Nine Memorial. The moment was somber, but her message was of hope and strength.
“When people walk through ... I don’t want them to only feel sorrow. I want them to feel a spark,” Ms. Sheppard said on Nov. 14. “It’s time to clear out the hatred, the racism, the division, and replace it with empathy, forgiveness, and enduring love.”
In the video accompanying this article, Chris Singleton says he refuses to let one man’s act of hate define his church. Instead, he says, “I’m going to spread love, and I’m going to spread unity.”
The memorial itself captures the essence of Ms. Sheppard’s words – and a wider commitment in this community that out of tragedy can come renewal and courage. The centerpiece of the memorial courtyard is the Fountain of Grace, a reflecting pool or basin with an opening in the shape of a cross at the pool’s center. The memorial’s website says the fountain serves as the “spiritual center of the courtyard, its flowing water evoking faith, life and renewal.”
Fellowship benches provide seating not far from where the names of the Emanuel nine are inscribed. The benches’ elongated marble sections look like angel’s wings wrapping around a community.
“Wherever you are, just give somebody a hug that’s standing next to you, and say ‘I love you’ while you’re at it,” Emanuel Nine Memorial Board Member Chris Singleton told those who gathered for the ribbon cutting. His mother, the Rev. Sharonda Coleman-Singleton, died in the shooting.
Mr. Singleton’s sense of forgiveness feels monumental. Back in 2015, he was a recent graduate of Goose Creek High School. Within two days after the shooting, he said of the 21-year-old white shooter that “we forgive, that’s one thing we are going to do.” That doesn’t mean the journey is easy. Years later, at the site of the memorial and of his mother’s murder, he spoke about the ethereal and things that are much heavier.
“When people go through stuff, especially young men, we’re expected to pack it down, and just get by,” Mr. Singleton said. “[Men] need hugs, too. We need to let it out, too. ... Stop pretending like it’s not affecting you.”
Functionally, the church known as Mother Emanuel is separate from the Mother Emanuel Memorial Foundation. Spiritually, there’s an understated bond between the healing work of the foundation and the journey that church and community members have undertaken over the last decade.
At the center of that is Deona Smith, a native of the region and executive director of the foundation, who has broad goals. “In some ways, balancing the foundation, families, and community has been easy because there’s alignment in a similar goal of honoring the Emanuel Nine and the survivors,” she writes via email. But also, “we hope to touch the lives of people of all races, religions, and backgrounds to be a catalyst for change.”
Where Ms. Sheppard and Mr. Singleton have been upfront in their emphasis on forgiveness and healing, the community’s progress has been neither simple nor uniform.
“I’ve learned over the years to never speak for the families and survivors. They are not monolithic and are at different stages of the grieving process,” Ms. Smith said.
Design architect Michael Arad has been tasked at least twice in a lifetime with the seemingly impossible – crafting a memorial to make sense of an unspeakable tragedy.
Back in 2003, Mr. Arad’s design for the National September 11 Memorial at the World Trade Center site was selected from more than 5,000 entries. The title of his design resonates with both 9/11 and the Mother Emanuel shooting – “Reflecting Absence.”
“In both instances, we tried to create places that welcome people in, that create a public realm that can act to bring us together and give us a sense of identity through community,” Mr. Arad said in an interview while attending the ribbon cutting. “We [don’t] confront these tragedies alone, but in the presence of others. And in doing so, we understand who we are and what our shared memories and responsibilities are.”
His design was inspired, in part, by the history of the church – a resilience that goes back long before the shooting, including an 1822 slave revolt led by one of the church founders.
“They put in the work over the past 11 years to build this beautiful, powerful memorial to the nine lives that were lost,” Sen.-elect Annie Andrews said in an interview at the event. “It’s also a reminder that South Carolinians are incredibly resilient, but there’s so much work to do.”
The Mother Emanuel Memorial Foundation is also planning for a Survivors’ Garden – a space where five trees and five benches will honor the living from that day, and a sixth bench will honor and respect the church itself.
Editor's note: This article was updated Nov. 19, the date of initial publication, to link to a video of Chris Singleton's 2015 statement about forgiveness, and to correct a time reference regarding his high school education.
